title: Computer-Use Agent Evaluated on OSWorld
tools: Python · OSWorld (desktop-task benchmark) · Claude · SubQ Snap decision model · Gemma 4 · OCR (optical character recognition) · Slurm on the OSU (Oregon State University) cluster · AWS (Amazon Web Services)
blurb: An agent that operates a Linux desktop; on 60 OSWorld (desktop task benchmark) tasks, a simple single-loop design scored 27, ahead of the planner stack's 16 and 20.
long: This project controls a real desktop given a natural-language goal. At each step, screen reading converts the screenshot to a list of numbered UI elements using OCR (optical character recognition) and the accessibility tree. Then a fast decision model selects the next action (~0.5 s). If it is uncertain, or the action requires text (e.g., typing or completing a task), a vision model (Claude) views the screenshot and chooses the action directly.

I evaluated it on OSWorld (a benchmark of actual desktop tasks performed in virtual machines), specifically the subset of 76 multi-app tasks that can be executed without requiring the OSWorld proxy. I divided these tasks into 15 development tasks, which were used for modifying the agent, and 60 testing tasks. My initial architecture was a planner stack: the system would plan out steps, verify each step against the screen, and replan if a step failed. The decision model by itself accomplished 0 out of the 60 testing tasks. The stack v2 achieved 16 successes (exact McNemar test p = 3.1e-5 compared to the decision model alone), while v3 achieved 20 successes. However, when comparing v3 to v2, there were 9 tasks that improved but 5 tasks that regressed, resulting in p = 0.42. This indicates that the difference falls within the range of variability observed between runs.

When I read through v3’s 40 failures, it was clear that the stack was causing many of the failures. 16 of the failures were cases where the stack’s done check said the task was complete, but OSWorld gave it a score of 0. There were also some checks that expected typed text that the OCR could not read, which caused 10 more runs to use the weaker fallback. So I replaced it with one loop with no planner, but I did add kept notes and a warning if the same action was taken repeatedly. That loop solved 27/60 tasks (average score 0.51). This is one run, and I designed the loop after reading the test task failures, so the 60 test tasks are not clean anymore. From then on I read the failures on the dev tasks only.

Other runs, measured:  On the 14 dev tasks, Opus 5.5 (medium effort) as the vision model: 8 solved (Sonnet 5: 7). Untrained Gemma 4 12B as fast decider: 2 solved. For a subset (10 tasks) of the more difficult OSWorld 2.0 (100 steps): 0/10 fully solved, average partial score 0.196. 9 out of 12 procedurally generated tasks (with custom checkers) were run (the VM failed to boot for 3) and all 9 were solved. These are not comparable to the OSWorld leaderboard, which uses the full task set and more steps.
highlights: 60 OSWorld (desktop-task benchmark) multi-app test tasks: decision model alone 0, stack v2 16, v3 20, one loop 27
v3 vs v2: p = 0.42 (exact McNemar test), within noise
Fast decider ~0.5 s per step; vision model ~5 s
OSWorld 2.0 sample: 0 of 10 fully completed, mean partial score 0.196
